blocks.text: Containers freeze the userland (runtime, system libraries, native wheels, your code) into an immutable, digest-addressed artifact that runs identically in dev, CI and prod.

items: Reproducibility: glibc, libpq, OpenSSL and native wheels are pinned; "works on my machine" usually means different system libraries.
Disposable dependencies: `docker compose up` gives everyone the same Postgres + pgvector + Qdrant in seconds.
Dev/prod parity: the tested artifact is the deployed artifact, identified by digest.
Side-by-side versions: Postgres 14 and 17 on one laptop without conflicts.
Universal deploy unit: Compose, Kubernetes, Cloud Run, ECS all run OCI images.
Model weights (hundreds of MB to GB): bake into the image or cache in a volume.
Embedding model and dimension must match between ingest and query; pinned images and model revisions prevent silent index drift.
Several stateful services: exactly Compose's shape.

blocks.text: Containers do not give you security, persistence or secret management by default. The writable layer dies with the container; root inside is root on the kernel unless you harden it.

Q: "Why containerize a RAG service?" A: "To pin the native ML stack and model revision so ingest and query embed identically, to run the vector DB and Postgres as reproducible dependencies, and to ship one immutable, digest-pinned artifact from dev to prod."

items: Image = frozen userland, addressed by digest.
Main wins: reproducibility, disposable dependencies, dev/prod parity.
RAG adds model-version coupling and large weights to manage.
Persistence, secrets and hardening are still your job.
